english.title: Stalking without fear / alarm / distress
english.standardoffencewording:

english.notes:
(i) Harassing a person may include alarming or causing the person distress; a "course of conduct" must involve conduct on at least two occasions and "conduct" includes speech.
(ii) Section 2A(2) of the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 sets out when a person's course of conduct amounts to stalking of another person. See subsection (3) for a non-exhaustive list of behaviours associated with stalking.
(iv) In section 1(1) of the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 the words 'another' and 'other' can be read in the plural. Where the harassment was aimed at two separate neighbours on different occasions (but all the incidents could be shown to be part of the same course of conduct), and both neighbours were named as complainants in a single indictment, that indictment was not duplicitous and was, therefore, valid. There did not have to be a separate indictment (or, by implication, police charge) per complainant (DPP v Dunn 2000)
(v) Section 360 of the Sentencing Act 2020 enables the sentencing court to impose a restraining order as well for the protection of the victim.(vi) For the racially / religiously aggravated version of this offence, see document H22540.(vii) Course of conduct. Incidents in cases of harassment must be so connected in type and in context as to justify the conclusion that they amounted to a course of conduct. See R v Patel [2004] EWCA Crim 3284
(viii) A course of conduct may include acts that occurred more than six months before the date on which the information was laid. This does not violate section 127 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 if the final event relied on occurred within the six months limitation period. DPP v Baker 2004.

other.penalty:
Summary: 51 weeks imprisonment and / or a fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale.

Note: The reference to 51 weeks is to be read as a reference to 6 months in relation to an offence committed before the commencement of section 281(5) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003.

Time limit for prosecutions:
6 months

On the 12th March 2015 the limit on fines imposed by a Magistrates’ court was removed – as such, the potential fine on summary conviction in relation to an offence committed after this date is unlimited.
